claim: The producer price index (PPI) was up [6.5%] year-over-year, per the most recent data as of [June 11, 2026]
quote: producers price index was up 6.5%
evidence: This is the May 2026 PPI reading (released ~June 11, the standard one-month lag), which CNBC reports as 6.5% YoY — the figure PPI fell from when June's reading (5.5%) was released in mid-July, after this video was published. Matches exactly.

claim: The consumer price index (CPI) was up [4.2%] year-over-year and core CPI (ex food/energy) was up [2.9%], per data released [June 10, 2026]
quote: up 4.2% and core, basically it's minus food and energy, and this is up 2.9%
evidence: This is the May 2026 CPI report (mid-June release). BLS's own June report explicitly frames the comparison: CPI 'increased 3.5% in June after increasing 4.2% in May,' core 'rose 2.6%, lagging the May rate of 2.9%.' Both May figures match exactly.

claim: Personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index was up [4.1%] and core PCE was up [3.4%] year-over-year, per data released [June 25, 2026]
quote: it went up 4.1% and our PCE core minus food and energy is up 3.4%
evidence: BEA's Personal Income and Outlays, May 2026 (released June 25): 'PCE price index for May increased 4.1 percent from the same month one year ago. Excluding food and energy, the PCE price index increased 3.4 percent.' Exact match.

claim: ADP reported private payrolls up [98,000] jobs in June 2026, concentrated in finance, education, health services, trade, transportation and utilities
quote: up 98,000 jobs in June
evidence: ADP's June 2026 report: private payrolls +98,000. Sector detail matches too — 'education and health services was the single largest contributor at 48,000...trade, transportation and utilities at 15,000...financial activities at 14,000' — the same industries the claim names.

claim: The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported [57,000] jobs added in June 2026, released [July 2, 2026]
quote: added 57,000 jobs in June
evidence: BLS Employment Situation, June 2026 (released July 2, 2026): nonfarm payrolls +57,000. Exact match.

claim: May 2026 payrolls were revised down by [43,000] jobs to [129,000]
quote: May is now at 129,000 jobs. This was just revised down by 43,000 jobs.
evidence: BLS June 2026 report: 'the change for May was revised down by 43,000, from +172,000 to +129,000.' Exact match, including the 129,000 landing figure.

claim: April 2026 payrolls were revised down by [31,000] jobs to [148,000]
quote: April is now at 148,000 jobs. This was also revised down by 31,000 jobs.
evidence: Same BLS release: 'the change for April was revised down by 31,000, from +179,000 to +148,000.' Exact match, including the 148,000 landing figure.

claim: Combined, April and May 2026 payrolls were revised down by [74,000] jobs from what was originally reported
quote: this is 74,000 jobs that don't exist that we thought existed
evidence: Arithmetic on claims 6 and 7: 43,000 + 31,000 = 74,000. The BLS release itself states the same total: 'Taken together, employment in April and May was 74,000 jobs lower than previously reported.'

claim: The labor force participation rate fell to [61.5%], down about [0.3 percentage points], per the June 2026 jobs report
quote: the labor force participation rate went down. It's now at 61.5%. It went down by about 0.3%
evidence: BLS/CNBC coverage of the June 2026 report: participation rate 'fell 0.3 percentage point to 61.5%, the lowest since March 2021.' Exact match.

claim: The US unemployment rate fell to a low of [3.4%], then climbed to about [4.3%-4.4%], and is now at [4.2%] as of the June 2026 report
quote: It was down at a low of 3.4% and then it's been climbing. It got up to about 4.3, 4.4%. It's down at 4.2%.
evidence: 3.4% was the BLS unemployment-rate low reached in 2023 (the lowest since 1969); the rate then rose into a 4.3%-4.4% band through 2025-early 2026 before the June 2026 report put it at 4.2% (helped down by the participation-rate drop in claim 9). The current-report figure and multi-year trend both check out.

claim: [7.1 million] people were counted as unemployed in the June 2026 report, defined as having actively looked for a job in the last 4 weeks
quote: There's 7.1 million people considered unemployed.
evidence: BLS: 'there were 7.1 million unemployed people in June 2026.' Exact match; the 4-week job-search definition given is BLS's standard U-3 definition.

claim: [6 million] people were not in the labor force because they had not looked for a job in the last 4 weeks, though they want one, as of the June 2026 report
quote: there's 6 million people not in the labor force cuz they haven't looked for a job in the last 4 weeks
evidence: Searched the BLS June 2026 release and its "not in labor force, want a job now" / marginally-attached tables; results surfaced the 7.1M unemployed and 4.7M part-time-for-economic-reasons figures (claims 11, 13) but not a standalone 6M figure for this specific category. Not contradicted, just not located in the search results reached.

claim: [4.7 million] people were working part-time but want full-time work, as of the June 2026 report
quote: that's another 4.7 million people that want that full-time work, but are currently part-time
evidence: BLS June 2026 release: 'the number of people employed part time for economic reasons changed little at 4.7 million.' Exact match.

claim: Adding the 7.1 million unemployed and 6 million not-in-labor-force-but-want-a-job figures gives [13.1 million] people who want a job
quote: you're at 13.1 million people that do want a job
evidence: 7.1M (claim 11, confirmed) + 6M (claim 12, unverifiable) = 13.1M — the arithmetic is correct, but it inherits claim 12's uncertainty: the 6M input to this sum was not independently located in search results.

claim: About [7.7%] of people are not employed but want a job, counting both those who have and haven't looked for work in the last 4 weeks
quote: there's about 7.7% of people that are not employed, but want a job
evidence: 13.1M (claim 14) as a share of an approximate ~170M labor-force-plus-marginally-attached base works out close to 7.7% (13.1/170 ≈ 7.7%) — the arithmetic is internally consistent, but rests on claim 14, which itself carries the unconfirmed 6M input from claim 12.

claim: Including people working part-time who want full-time work, closer to [10.5%] of people want a full-time job they don't have, as of the June 2026 data
quote: is closer to about 10 and 1/2%
evidence: Adding the 4.7M part-time-for-economic-reasons group (claim 13, confirmed) to the 7.7% base (claim 15) is arithmetically consistent with landing near 10.5%, but the figure still inherits the unconfirmed 6M input several steps upstream (claim 12).

claim: About [one in four] unemployed people have been unemployed for at least 6 months (27 weeks) or more, as of the June 2026 data
quote: it's about one in four people have been unemployed for at least 6 months or more
evidence: BLS data for June 2026 puts the long-term-unemployed (27+ weeks) share at 27.3% of all unemployed. 27.3% rounds fairly to 'about one in four' (25%) — a reasonable colloquial approximation, not an exact match.

claim: The JOLTS report released [June 30, 2026] showed [7.6 million] job openings
quote: There were 7.6 million jobs reported as being open and available.
evidence: BLS JOLTS release, June 30 2026 (covering May 2026 data): 'job openings was unchanged at 7.6 million in May.' Exact match.

claim: The same JOLTS report showed [5.2 million] people were hired
quote: 5.2 million people were hired
evidence: Same release: 'hires were unchanged at 5.2 million.' Exact match.

claim: The same JOLTS report showed [5.1 million] people separated from employment
quote: 5.1 million people separated from their employment
evidence: Same release: 'total separations changed little at 5.1 million.' Exact match.

claim: The gap between JOLTS openings and hires means about [2.4 million] jobs are left unfilled, roughly a third of open jobs each month
quote: That's about 2.4 million jobs are left unfilled. It's approximately about a third of jobs are left open each month.
evidence: 7.6M openings (claim 18) − 5.2M hires (claim 19) = 2.4M, exactly as stated. 2.4M / 7.6M ≈ 31.6%, which rounds fairly to 'about a third.'

claim: The FOMC held interest rates steady at [3.5%-3.75%] at its [June 17, 2026] meeting
quote: hold interest rates steady at 3.5% to 3.75%
evidence: FOMC voted 12-0 to hold the federal funds rate at 3.50%-3.75% on June 17, 2026 — the fourth consecutive hold, and Kevin Warsh's first meeting as Fed chair. Exact match.

claim: The new Fed chair effectively reframed the Fed's 2% inflation target, suggesting only the first digit matters (so 2.5% or 2.9% would be acceptable), around the [June 17, 2026] meeting
quote: He said really it's the first number that matters.
evidence: Three separate searches (June 17 2026 press conference, July 2026 congressional testimony, August 2026 Jackson Hole speech) find Chair Warsh consistently affirming 2% as a firm, unmoved target — at the June 17 presser itself he said the Fed has 'the capability and commitment to deliver on our price-stability objective of 2 percent... that's exactly what we're going to do,' and at Jackson Hole (Aug 28) called 2% a 'firm and fixed' target and said inflation 'isn't slowing' enough. No source found any 'first digit' reframing; the available record contradicts it directly.

claim: In the Fed's June 2026 dot plot, [17 of 18] FOMC participants expected the interest rate to hold steady or rise by the end of 2026
quote: 17 out of the 18 people that were looking at this, providing the data, have said they expect it to stay the same or go up
evidence: The June 17 2026 Summary of Economic Projections: 9 of 18 participants project a hike by year-end, 1 projects a cut, and by elimination 8 project a hold. Hold-or-higher = 9 + 8 = 17 of 18 — exactly the figure claimed, even though the underlying breakdown (9 hike / 8 hold / 1 cut) isn't literally 'expect to stay the same or go up' phrased that way.

claim: At the June 2026 meeting, the Fed said it wants to maintain ample reserves by buying 0-to-3-year Treasury bills
quote: They said that they want to maintain ample reserves. Basically, they're buying up that 0 to 3-year T-bills
evidence: Fed's July 2026 Monetary Policy Report confirms the Committee reaffirmed the 'ample reserves' balance-sheet policy at the June meeting and has continued reserve-management Treasury bill purchases since January 2026. Matches.

claim: First-quarter 2026 GDP was revised to [2.1%], per data released [June 25, 2026]
quote: first quarter 2026 was revised to 2.1%
evidence: BEA's third estimate of Q1 2026 GDP, released June 25 2026, revised growth up to 2.1% from 1.6% in the second estimate. Exact match.

claim: The Atlanta Fed's GDPNow tracker dropped its second-quarter 2026 GDP estimate significantly, to [+1.2%], as of [July 1, 2026]
quote: GDP now has dropped their estimate fairly significantly. We're only at plus 1.2%
evidence: Atlanta Fed: 'On July 1, the GDPNow model nowcast of real GDP growth in Q2 2026 is 1.2%,' down from a prior 2.5% reading. Exact match, including the 'dropped significantly' framing.

claim: Personal income rose [0.7%], or [$181 billion], per data released [June 25, 2026]
quote: personal income is up 0.7% up 181 billion
evidence: BEA: 'Personal income increased $181.6 billion (0.7 percent at a monthly rate) in May.' Exact match.

claim: Personal consumption expenditures (spending) rose [0.7%], or [$156 billion], per data released [June 25, 2026]
quote: Personal consumption expenditures are also up 0.7%... it went up by 156 billion dollars
evidence: BEA: 'PCE increased $156.1 billion (0.7 percent) in May.' Exact match.

claim: The personal savings rate is at about [3%], per data released [June 25, 2026]
quote: the personal savings rate is going up slightly. It's at 3%
evidence: BEA: 'the personal saving rate...was 3.0 percent' for May 2026. Exact match.

claim: The University of Michigan index of consumer sentiment was up [10.5%] month-over-month and down [18.5%] year-over-year, per data released [June 26, 2026]
quote: Month-over-month, we're up 10.5%. Year-over-year, we're down 18.5%
evidence: The final June 2026 reading of 49.5 is reported as a 10.5% (4.7 point) rise, and secondary coverage describes it as 'nearly 20% less than a year ago' — consistent with the claimed 18.5% YoY decline. The MoM comparison base in some secondary write-ups is described as April rather than May, a minor ambiguity that doesn't change the headline figures.

claim: The University of Michigan's current economic conditions sub-index was up [4.1%] month-over-month and down [26.4%] year-over-year
quote: Current economic conditions, we're up 4.1% down 26.4% year-over-year
evidence: 'The Current Economic Conditions Index rose...to 47.7, representing a 4.1% increase from the previous month but a 26.4% drop from a year ago.' Exact match.

claim: The University of Michigan's index of consumer expectations was up [15%] month-over-month and down [12.7%] year-over-year
quote: Index of consumer expectations, we're up 15% month-over-month down 12.7% year-over-year
evidence: 'Consumer Expectations rose...to 50.7, representing a 15.0% increase from the previous month but a 12.7% drop from one year ago.' Exact match.

claim: June 2026 was the first time since 2022 that more consumers rated their current financial situation as bad rather than good, per University of Michigan data
quote: This is the first time I've seen this crossover since 2022
evidence: Search located June 2026 'better/worse off' figures (56% worse, 19% better) but no source clearly dated the last time worse-off exceeded better-off by this margin; one AI-synthesized summary suggested 'since June 2025' rather than 2022, which conflicts with the claim rather than confirming it. Named gap: the specific historical comparison point was not located in a citable primary table.

claim: Construction spending increased [0.1%] month-over-month (±0.7 percentage points) and fell [1.5%] year-over-year (±1.3 percentage points), per data released [July 1, 2026]
quote: construction spending increased by 0.1%... it could be as much as plus or minus 0.7%... year-over-year, it's down 1.5% with an error plus or minus 1.3%
evidence: Census Bureau, May 2026 construction spending: '0.1 percent above the revised April estimate...1.5 percent below the May 2025 estimate,' with the standard published margin of error of ±1.3 percentage points on the year-over-year change. MoM and YoY headline figures and the YoY margin match exactly; the MoM margin (±0.7 pts) is consistent with Census's standard reporting format but wasn't independently isolated in search results.

claim: US manufacturing was expanding overall in June 2026 but at a slower pace than the prior month, per the ISM Manufacturing PMI
quote: manufacturing is expanding, but they're growing at a slower pace
evidence: ISM Manufacturing PMI came in at 53.3 in June 2026, down from 54.0 in May — still in expansion (above 50) but a slower rate of growth. Exact match.

claim: The ISM's employment sub-index has been in contraction for a while, as of the June 2026 report
quote: Employment's been contracting for a while.
evidence: ISM's Employment Index registered 49.7% in June 2026 (still below the 50% breakeven, i.e. in contraction), its 33rd consecutive month of contraction. Confirmed.

claim: June 2026 was the first month in some time that the ISM's new orders sub-index actually contracted
quote: New orders, this is the first month it's actually contracted in some time.
evidence: The opposite happened: ISM's New Orders Index registered 56.0% in June 2026 — in expansion, and the sixth consecutive month of expansion after four straight months of contraction earlier in the year. Two independent searches on this specific figure returned the same reading, so this isn't a thin result: new orders were expanding, not newly contracting.

claim: About [20%] of the world's oil passes through the Strait of Hormuz
quote: about 20% of the world's oil goes through this area
evidence: Reporting on the 2026 Strait of Hormuz crisis consistently cites the strait carrying 'around 20 million barrels of oil per day, representing roughly 20% of global seaborne oil trade.' Matches.

claim: As of early July 2026, the Strait of Hormuz was being blockaded by Iran, and Middle Eastern countries were building pipelines to route around it
quote: this is leading Iran to blockade the Strait of Hormuz... they are building pipelines to try to circumvent this whole issue
evidence: The situation was genuinely volatile at exactly this moment: a June 17 2026 US-Iran memorandum had established a 60-day safe-passage arrangement, but it broke down after ships were attacked July 6-7 and Trump declared the truce over, with the strait becoming 'effectively closed to routine commercial shipping' by early July. The video's own hedge ('on again, off again... hard to keep up with') fairly captures this fluid state rather than asserting a clean, static blockade.

claim: The US Strategic Petroleum Reserve was dropping below [320 million barrels], its lowest level in about 40 years / since the 1980s, as of early July 2026
quote: this is now dropping below 320 million barrels, and dropping each day now... it's the lowest it's been in about 40 years
evidence: SPR levels were declining through 2026, reaching 311.4M barrels by mid-July and 308M by August — consistent with a level 'dropping below 320 million...and dropping each day' in early July, on its way to the lowest level since 1983 (43 years, i.e. 'about 40 years'). Directionally and numerically confirmed.

claim: Morgan Stanley started limiting withdrawals from a private credit fund in 2026
quote: Morgan Stanley has started to limit some of their withdrawals
evidence: Bloomberg, June 23 2026: Morgan Stanley capped withdrawals at its $7 billion North Haven private credit fund at 5% after investors sought to redeem 11.6% of shares in Q2 2026. Confirmed, and recent enough to be current news as of this video's publish date.

claim: SpaceX completed an IPO in summer 2026
quote: we had SpaceX come out
evidence: SpaceX priced its IPO on June 11 2026 and began trading on Nasdaq (ticker SPCX) June 12 2026, closing at ~$85.7B raised. Confirmed.

claim: Gold was trading at [$4,193] per ounce, as of early July 2026
quote: currently gold is trading at $4,193 per ounce
evidence: July 2026 gold traded in a $3,963-$4,199.70 range per troy ounce — the claimed $4,193 sits inside that range, close to the month's high. Best-reachable source for the specific figure is a price-tracking aggregator (tier 4), which caps this at plausible rather than confirmed.

claim: The US government's own gold holdings are valued at the statutory price of [$42] per ounce, worth about [$11 billion] at that price
quote: all of the US gold that the US holds is at $42 an ounce
evidence: The statutory price of gold has been fixed at $42.22 (42 2/9 dollars) per fine troy ounce since 1973. The Treasury holds about 261.5 million ounces, which at $42.22/oz values the reserve at ~$11.04 billion — matching the video's 'I think it's 11 something billion.'

claim: Revaluing US gold reserves from the statutory $42/oz price to the current market price would yield a gain of roughly [$1.1-1.2 trillion]
quote: I think it's 11 something billion dollars worth of gold at the current legal valuation... gaining a little bit more than 1.1 trillion uh in gains which is 1.2 trillion uh dollars effectively
evidence: Shown sum: 261.5M oz x $4,193/oz (claim 44) ≈ $1,096.5B market value; minus the ~$11.04B statutory book value (claim 45) ≈ $1,085.5B (~$1.09T) gain. That's close to, but modestly below, the claimed 'a little more than 1.1 trillion...1.2 trillion' — the two figures the speaker gives in the same breath also disagree with each other by about $100B, which is itself evidence the number is a rough gesture rather than a precise calculation.

claim: FDIC deposit insurance covers deposits up to about [$250,000] per depositor
quote: insured up to their limit of about 250,000
evidence: FDIC: deposits insured up to $250,000 per depositor, per insured bank, per ownership category — unchanged in 2026. Exact match.
